identity.title: Global URL Shortener
identity.prompt: Design infrastructure for a global URL shortening service. It must absorb heavy redirect traffic, accept new links, survive a viral short URL, and stay within latency, capacity headroom, and monthly budget — without a prescribed topology.

narrative.hook: You're handed LinkVault's startup MVP (~12k RPS) the day #MegaDrop2026 goes viral. Traffic is now 124k RPS sustained on an $85k/mo board — fix and scale it.
narrative.stakes: The inherited MVP fails on first Run. Scale what is already on the canvas until every scored target passes.
briefingBeats: Demand is global: six regions share 120k redirects/sec; latency is traffic-weighted p95, so one continent is not enough.
A viral short code concentrates 30k redirect RPS on one key — hot-key pressure is separate from aggregate throughput.
Budget is $85k/mo including CDN usage and cross-region transfer; spray-and-pray sizing fails, efficient layered designs pass.
Placement changes how much work each piece absorbs for this workload — edge vs read-aside vs origin — without prescribing a single diagram.

components.whyHere: Challenge-owned demand injector for the viral URL-shortener workload.
pros: Defines sustained redirect and write demand for the level
Carries geographic origin shares without player knobs
cons: Not configurable — you cannot dial traffic down to make the board easier
commonMistakes: Expecting traffic-source knobs or treating it as a priced component
components.placementIntent: Challenge-owned ingress of demand; always the start of the request path

components.whyHere: Nearest-healthy region routing when you place regional service capacity.
pros: Steers users toward nearby healthy deployments
Pays off when traffic spans continents
cons: Does not replace caches or database capacity
commonMistakes: Dropping a router with a single-region MVP and expecting geo magic
Placing it after regional pools instead of before them
components.placementIntent: Before regional service pools on the user path; geo payoff needs multi-region compute

components.whyHere: Fan-out across a service pool so capacity and HA can scale horizontally.
pros: Spreads request load across multiple service instances
Equal or capacity-weighted split is an explicit tradeoff
cons: Single upstream ≈ almost no fan-out payoff
Adds real monthly cost even when topology is weak
commonMistakes: Paying for an LB in front of one service instance
Expecting failure-aware backend exclusion that Level 1 does not fake
components.placementIntent: On the request path in front of a multi-instance service pool
components.costNotes: Non-zero educational monthly cost — every LB is a budget tradeoff

components.whyHere: Stateless redirect and write compute on the request path.
cons: A hot region can fail while global instance totals look fine
Miss traffic from weak edge cache still pounds origin compute
commonMistakes: Undersizing the inherited MVP under viral load
Ignoring regional placement when geography is active
components.placementIntent: Compute on the active request path between edge/ingress and data stores
components.costNotes: Per-instance size tiers drive monthly cost; more instances raise the bill linearly

components.whyHere: Edge offload for average redirects — the high-leverage cache for this workload.
pros: Strong absorb of cacheable redirects when sitting on the user path
Coverage and TTL band control eligibility and hit intent
cons: Usage pricing at 124k RPS is a major budget line
Weak when placed behind Service instead of at the edge
commonMistakes: Putting CDN after Service and expecting edge leverage
Skipping CDN to save base cost while exploding origin load and latency
components.placementIntent: Edge ingress before Service on the user → origin path; average-redirect workhorse
components.costNotes: Tier base ($2k–$12k) plus usage projected from sustained incoming RPS

components.whyHere: Read-aside data cache and viral-key relief valve beside the database — not a substitute for edge CDN.
pros: Helps repeated/hot-key reads that reach the store path
Hot-key capacity is modeled separately from aggregate utilization
cons: Limited average redirect offload versus CDN on this workload
Regional footprints do not sync across regions
commonMistakes: Using Redis as an edge CDN on the user path
Max-dialing Redis and expecting it to carry most average redirects
Assuming replicated mode shards a single viral key
components.placementIntent: Read-aside beside Postgres on the service read path — viral relief valve, not the average-redirect main character
components.costNotes: Tier + standalone/replicated mode; each regional footprint is independent base cost

components.whyHere: Durable row store for link data; primary owns writes and viral-key read pressure.
pros: Authoritative storage for redirects and new links
Read replicas add aggregate read capacity
cons: Viral hot-key reads count against primary read capacity — replicas do not shard one key
commonMistakes: Expecting replicas to fix a single viral short code
Ignoring write headroom while only scaling reads
components.placementIntent: Primary durable store on the read_write path; replicas for aggregate reads only
components.costNotes: Primary tier plus per-replica cost; remote replicas also drive replication transfer

unscoredTargets.label: Availability
unscoredTargets.reason: Deferred until truthful resilience and failure semantics exist. Not scored in Phase 2.

scoring.hotKeyGateNote: 30k RPS on one short code must not saturate Redis hot-path capacity or Postgres primary reads — the hot-key gate is separate from aggregate throughput.

edge_cache.note: Redirects are highly edge-cacheable when CDN sits on the user path.

data_cache.note: In-memory cache helps hot keys beside the DB; weak as a substitute for edge cache.

request_fanout.note: Load balancing pays off when multiple healthy upstreams exist on path.

geo_routing.note: Routing matters when traffic spans regions.

bands.notes: When correctly placed at edge — highest average-redirect absorb share
Read-aside: quiet on average redirects; may wake on viral beat. Idle or misplaced Redis should stay near 0–0.02 share.
Service traffic after edge miss — stays visibly busy when caches are weak
Miss path + writes; primary stressed on viral key (replicas do not shard one code). Idle/unused store-path absorb stays near zero.

firstRunExpectation.summary: Inherited MVP (medium×3 Service in us-east + medium Postgres, no replicas) is undersized for 124k viral load — throughput, latency, and headroom fail, and the hot-key gate fails on primary pressure.

playtestChecklist: Users→Service→Postgres only — fails for the right reasons; traffic visibly pounds origin.
Redis max dials, read-aside — helps some; not a free pass; some traffic visibly through Redis, most still onward as ceiling allows.
Same Redis dials, misplaced / edge — clearly worse and quieter on the canvas.
CDN on path — more leverage than Redis for average redirects; CDN path looks busier than Redis for the same workload.
Viral/hot-key — pressures primary; read-aside Redis helps hot path more than tiny/misplaced Redis (metrics + visuals).
LB/router — payoff only when topology warrants.
Budget trap: overbuilt active Redis/CDN without need still painful.
Cheapest room: lean good design can approach ~0.5× budget; fat design fails.
Idle extra: add off-path Redis under budget to a passing design → still passes; game tells you it is unused.
Future/N/A until object storage ships: same primary role, object_store affinity worse $ / latency than durable_store — no slug branch.
